discoveryHook.scenario: You're a medical researcher. You need to find out if a new drug lowers blood pressure. Do you just observe people who happen to take it? Do you give it to some and compare to others? The way you collect data determines whether your conclusions will be trusted. Welcome to the art of data collection — where asking the right question is only half the battle.

formulaCard.title: Choosing a Method

legend.meaning: The study's goal determines the best method.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Method} = \begin{cases} \text{Observational} & \text{if only watching} \\ \text{Experiment} & \text{if applying a treatment} \\ \text{Simulation} & \text{if real study is impossible/dangerous} \\ \text{Survey} & \text{if asking opinions/facts} \end{cases}$$

rows.1: Use a model to mimic reality
rows.2: Crash test dummies in car safety tests

explanation: There are four main methods of data collection: [[kw:observational study]], [[kw:experiment]], [[kw:simulation]], and [[kw:survey]].
In an [[kw:observational study]], a researcher observes and measures characteristics without influencing the subjects. No treatment is applied.
In an [[kw:experiment]], a treatment is applied to part of a population, and responses are observed. A control group may receive a placebo.
A [[kw:simulation]] uses a mathematical or physical model to reproduce a situation, often when real study is impractical or dangerous.
A [[kw:survey]] collects data by asking questions, often through interviews, mail, or phone. Question wording must be neutral to avoid bias.

teacherCues: Show a picture of a researcher observing animals in the wild vs. a lab experiment. Ask: 'What's the difference between watching and intervening?'
Write the four methods on the board: Observational Study, Experiment, Simulation, Survey. Ask students to match each to a real-world example.

confusionCorner.title: Survey Bias — It's All in the Wording
confusionCorner.body: A survey question that suggests an answer can lead to biased results. For example, 'Do you agree that whole grains improve health?' is leading. Better: 'How do you think whole grains affect health?' [[imp:Neutral wording is crucial.]]

explanation: A well-designed experiment must have three key elements: [[kw:control]], [[kw:randomization]], and [[kw:replication]].
[[kw:Control]] means limiting the effects of variables other than the treatment. A control group often receives a [[kw:placebo]].
[[kw:Randomization]] randomly assigns subjects to treatment or control groups to reduce bias.
[[kw:Replication]] is repeating the experiment under the same or similar conditions to verify results. A larger sample size increases reliability.
A [[kw:confounding variable]] occurs when an outside factor influences the response and you can't tell which factor caused the effect.
[[kw:Blinding]] means subjects don't know if they receive real treatment; double‑blind means neither subjects nor experimenters know until after data collection.

rows.2: Using a placebo for the control group
Coin flip decides treatment or control

steps: The sample size is only 10 subjects, which is very small.
A valid experiment requires [[kw:replication]] — more subjects to ensure the result isn't due to chance.
Improvement: Use a much larger sample, e.g., 1,000 subjects, to improve reliability.

confusionCorner.title: Placebo vs. Hawthorne Effect
confusionCorner.body: The [[imp:placebo effect]] is a positive response to an inactive treatment due to belief. The [[imp:Hawthorne effect]] is a change in behavior simply because subjects know they're being observed. Both can bias results; blinding helps control them.

discoveryHook.scenario: A coffee shop owner remodels with bright colors and, coincidentally, a new mall opens next door. Business goes up. Did the colors help? The mall's opening is a confounding variable — you can't separate the effects. Good experimental design uses control, randomization, and replication to avoid such confusion.

formulaCard.title: Choosing a Sampling Method
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Method} = \begin{cases} \text{SRS} & \text{if simple and unbiased needed} \\ \text{Stratified} & \text{if key subgroups must be included} \\ \text{Cluster} & \text{if natural groups exist, pick whole groups} \\ \text{Systematic} & \text{if a list exists and you want simplicity} \end{cases}$$

rows.2: When you have a complete list and need unbiased sample

rows.1: Split into strata, then random within each
rows.2: When groups differ and you want each represented

rows.3: Clusters must be similar to each other

rows.1: Pick every k‑th after random start
rows.2: Quick and easy when ordering exists
rows.3: Risk of pattern in the data

explanation: A [[kw:census]] collects data from an entire population. Often impractical, so we use sampling.
A [[kw:simple random sample]] (SRS) gives every member an equal chance, and every possible sample of the same size has an equal chance. Use random number tables or generators.
[[kw:Stratified sampling]] divides the population into subgroups (strata) sharing a characteristic, then takes a random sample from each stratum. Ensures representation across groups.

[[kw:Cluster sampling]] divides the population into naturally occurring clusters (e.g., zip codes, classrooms), then randomly selects one or more clusters and includes all members from those clusters.
[[kw:Systematic sampling]] assigns numbers, randomly chooses a start, and selects every k‑th member. Easy to use but can miss patterns.
[[kw:Convenience sampling]] uses readily available subjects — it's quick but often biased.

confusionCorner.body: Both divide the population into groups, but in stratified sampling you take a sample [[imp:from every]] stratum; in cluster sampling you take [[imp:all members]] from only some clusters. Stratified ensures each subgroup is represented; cluster is a shortcut that can miss subgroups if clusters aren't diverse.
confusionCorner.title: Stratified ≠ Cluster

Explain to a partner: Why would you choose stratified sampling here instead of cluster?
steps: Splitting by class year and sampling within each is [[kw:stratified sampling]] — you're ensuring representation from each class.
Randomly choosing entire dormitories and surveying everyone in them is [[kw:cluster sampling]].
Stratified is better when class year opinions might differ; cluster is easier if students in each dorm are similar.
The selection uses a fixed interval (every 50th) after a random start.
This is [[kw:systematic sampling]].
It's efficient but must be checked for patterns in the production process.

discoveryHook.scenario: You need to survey students' opinions about cafeteria food. You could randomly select 100 students from the entire roster, or pick a few entire homerooms, or line them up and take every 10th student. Each method has strengths and weaknesses. Choosing the right sampling technique is critical to getting a representative picture.

confusionCorner.title: Block ≠ Stratified, Matched ≠ Just Two Groups
confusionCorner.body: Blocking is for experiments; stratified sampling is for surveys. In a matched‑pairs design, it's not enough to just have two groups — they must be deliberately paired on a relevant characteristic. [[imp:Random assignment within pairs or block is essential.]]

explanation: Beyond the basic completely randomized design, we use [[kw:randomized block design]] when subjects have known characteristics that affect response (e.g., age, gender).
In a randomized block design, subjects are divided into blocks (like strata), and then within each block, randomly assigned to treatments. This controls for the blocking variable.
A [[kw:matched‑pairs design]] pairs subjects based on similarity, then one receives Treatment A and the other Treatment B. Or the same subject is measured under both treatments (before/after).
These designs reduce variability due to extraneous factors, making the treatment effect easier to detect.

rows.1: Divide into blocks (e.g., age groups), randomize within each
rows.2: Weight‑loss drink tested on 30‑39, 40‑49, 50+ age groups

rows.1: Pair similar subjects, randomly assign treatments; or same subject receives both

blocks.title: Advanced Designs: Blocks and Matched Pairs

discoveryHook.scenario: Testing a new sunscreen? Pair subjects by skin type, then randomly assign one to the new formula and one to the old. Or measure the same person's skin before and after application. These advanced designs — blocking and matched pairs — squeeze out more precise results by controlling for individual differences.

confusionCorner.body: Rushing to collect data without a clear plan leads to wasted effort and unreliable conclusions. Always define your population, variables, method, and design before the first data point is collected. [[imp:A well‑designed study is replicable and defensible.]]
confusionCorner.title: Don't Skip the Blueprint!

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Designing a Statistical Study

discoveryHook.scenario: You're asked to design a study on whether a new teaching method improves test scores. Where do you start? The blueprint — Understand, Solve, Conclude — guides you: define your population and variables, choose data collection and sampling methods, design the experiment, then analyze and interpret. A solid plan leads to solid conclusions.

examples.prompt: Design a study to test the effect of sleep deprivation on motor skills. Eighteen volunteers are available.
examples.title: Example A – Design a Study (Sleep Deprivation)
steps: Understand: Variable = motor skill score; population = volunteers (assume representativeness).

Solve (Design): Perform an [[kw:experiment]]. Randomly assign 9 subjects to the treatment group (stay awake 24 hours) and 9 to control (normal sleep). Use random number generator for assignment. Use a placebo‑controlled, double‑blind if possible (though hard with sleep).
Solve (Details): Ensure all subjects follow same protocols except sleep. Measure motor skills with a standardized test.
Conclude: After experiment, compare group means, infer whether sleep deprivation affects motor skills, note small sample size as limitation.

examples.prompt: You want to survey college students' study habits at a large university. Describe a sampling plan using stratified sampling.
steps: Understand: Population = all enrolled students; variable = study hours.
Solve: Use [[kw:stratified sampling]] with strata = class year (freshman, sophomore, junior, senior) because study habits may differ by year.
Randomly select, say, 50 students from each stratum. This guarantees representation from each class year.
Conclude: If a simple random sample happened to miss seniors, results might be skewed; stratified prevents that.
examples.title: Example B – Choosing Sampling for a Survey
examples.peerPrompt:

Explain to a partner: What strata would you use, and why would stratified be better than a simple random sample?

examples.prompt: A researcher wants to know if a new vitamin boosts memory. She recruits 20 people from a gym, gives them the vitamin, and after a month tests their memory with a crossword puzzle. All do well. Identify flaws in the design.
steps: Understand: Variable = memory performance; population = gym members (convenience sample).

Solve (Design): No control group — all received the vitamin, so no comparison. No randomization. Small sample size. The test (crossword puzzle) may not be a valid measure. Subjects may have improved due to practice, not the vitamin.

Conclude: The study lacks control, randomization, replication. A better design: randomly assign a larger, representative sample to vitamin or placebo, use a validated memory test, and blind participants.
examples.title: Example C – Identifying Flaws

rows.2: Population: all students at a school; variable: test score
Method: experiment; design: randomized block by grade level

rows.1: Collect data, analyze, interpret, check errors
rows.2: Compute means, run hypothesis test, state margin of error

explanation: Designing a statistical study follows a logical sequence: Understand → Solve → Conclude.
Step 1 – [[kw:Understand]]: Identify the variable(s) of interest, the population, and the goal. What do you want to know?

Step 2 – [[kw:Solve]]: Develop a plan. Choose method of data collection (observational, experiment, survey, simulation). If sampling, select an appropriate technique (SRS, stratified, cluster, systematic). If experimenting, decide on design (completely randomized, block, matched pairs). Ensure control, randomization, replication.
Step 3 – [[kw:Conclude]]: Collect data, describe it with descriptive statistics, then use inferential statistics to make decisions. Identify possible errors or biases.

Examples: blood pressure, test score, opinion.

title: Data Collection and Experimental Design
presenterNotes: In Block 1, emphasize the distinction between observational studies and experiments. Use the coffee shop confounding example to preview the next block.
Block 2 covers the heart of experimental design. The three pillars (control, randomization, replication) should be memorized. The blinding and placebo concepts are essential.
Block 3 walks through all major sampling techniques. Use props or drawings to illustrate stratified vs. cluster. The confusion corner note on stratified vs. cluster is key.
Block 4 introduces randomized block and matched pairs. Relate block design to stratified sampling from Block 3. The twin example makes matched pairs memorable.

The Blueprint Aid (Block 5) ties everything together. Use the six‑step guideline from the textbook but adapt to the Understand‑Solve‑Conclude format. Encourage students to apply the blueprint to any study they encounter.
